derives_from: **`te__te-IN.json`**, by a character shift rather than a rewrite: Kannada's codepoints are Telugu's + 0x80 exactly, both blocks being ISCII-ordered, and all 60 Telugu characters that table emits shift to an assigned Kannada codepoint of the same Unicode name -- checked against `unicodedata`, with an assertion in `tmp/kn/build_respell.py` that raises on the first one that does not. Telugu's own derivation from Hindi hit two unassigned codepoints and had to override them by hand; this one hits none. The two scripts also share the whole mechanism the table is about -- a consonant letter that already says [a], so three spellings per consonant and `spellSlot` choosing on what the syllable has already emitted -- and, unlike Devanagari, both write every vowel they pronounce and neither deletes the word-final inherent one. **Kittel's *A Kannada-English Dictionary* (Basel Mission, 1894) and the University of Madras *Kannada-English Dictionary*** on DSAL fix which letter an educated Kannada reader expects for a foreign sound: ಫ for /f/, ಜ for /z/, no nukta anywhere. `content/RESPELL-SYSTEMS.md` names no Kannada pronunciation key and no published one was found -- Kannada lexicography prints no respelling column, because the orthography is shallow enough not to need one, which is the same reason Gujarati's, Hungarian's and Czech's entries say what they say -- so what is adapted is stated here rather than cited. The loanword spellings that decide the hard cases are Kannada's own and are checkable on any newspaper page: ಫೋನ್, ಬ್ಯಾಂಕ್, ಪ್ಲಾಟ್ಫಾರ್ಮ್, ಜೀರೋ, ಎಟಿಎಂ, ವೈ-ಫೈ.

deviations.why: Replaced with the same four rules `r` has, which repairs a live defect in the table this derives from. Telugu gives `r̝` an `onset` rule with no `after_out` condition plus an `any` rule, and `spellSlot` takes the first matching rule in array order -- so the `onset` rule fires for the *second* consonant of an onset cluster too, and Czech `přes` /pr̝es/ prints `పరెస్` in Telugu, pa-res, with the virama missing. Gujarati gave `r̝` the same rules as its own `r` and prints `પ્રેસ` correctly. Eight rows of the Czech pack reach it. Here the fix is load-bearing twice over: Noto Serif Kannada throws in this project's shaper on an independent vowel followed by a bare virama, so a rule that can emit a leading `್` after a hiatus nucleus is a crash rather than a misspelling.

deviations.rule: Hindi's word-final virama strip, which Telugu deleted
deviations.why: Stays deleted. Devanagari deletes a word-final inherent vowel categorically, so Hindi's टेस्ट and बैंक carry no final virama and its table strips one. **Kannada is on Telugu's side of that line and not Gujarati's**: every vowel Kannada pronounces is written, so a final consonant *must* keep its virama -- which is why the language writes ಫೋನ್, ಪಾಸ್ಪೋರ್ಟ್ and ಟಿಕೆಟ್, and why this pack's own `ipa` column, derived independently by espeak, ends those words in a consonant. Gujarati was the first Brahmic table after Hindi's to keep the strip; this is the second to refuse it.

deviations.rule: Telugu's undoing of Hindi's four vowel-length collapses
deviations.why: Carried over unchanged, and it is the largest thing this table does that Hindi's cannot. Kannada writes all five length pairs with a dependent sign for both members -- ಅ/ಆ ಇ/ಈ ಉ/ಊ ಎ/ಏ ಒ/ಓ -- so /i/ is ಇ/ಿ against /iː/ ಈ/ೀ, /e/ is ಎ/ೆ against /eː/ ಏ/ೇ, /o/ is ಒ/ೊ against /oː/ ಓ/ೋ. `policy.length` is `none` because the script carries the length and a bare `ː` has nothing left to do. Telugu needed two hand-written overrides here (U+0C11 and U+0C49 are unassigned in Telugu, so Hindi's ऑ/ॉ could not be shifted); Kannada needs none, because it inherits Telugu's answer rather than Hindi's problem.

deviations.rule: /a/ against /aː/, which is the one pair deliberately *not* undone
deviations.why: Short a has no dependent sign in Kannada any more than in Telugu or Devanagari, so /a/ -> "" would emit nothing in a nucleus and every `aX` diphthong would lose its first vowel -- Mandarin 好 /xɑʊ/ coming out with one vowel where the word has two, which is the defect `tmp/ta/nuclei.mjs` found and paid eleven hand-written rules for. So /a aː ɑ ɑː ə ɐ ʌ/ all take ಆ/ಾ and a reader gets a row one length-mark too long rather than one vowel short.

Absent, as in Telugu. U+0CBC exists and appears in no Kannada text, no newspaper and no shipped face's real usage; standard Kannada writes loan /f/ as ಫ and loan /z/ as ಜ -- ಫೋನ್, ಫಾರ್ಮ್, ಜೀರೋ, ಜೋನ್. Implemented by the source table dropping the character, which also takes ड़/ढ़ to ಡ/ಢ, Kannada having no retroflex flap. The cost is that /f/ collides with /pʰ/, which Telugu's entry records and which no Kannada orthography can avoid.

approximations: Sounds with no Kannada letter, and what they get. Kannada's own inventory is large -- the whole four-way stop series, both retroflex and dental nasals, three sibilants, five vowel-length pairs -- so the list is shorter than Hindi's and every entry on it is inherited from that table rather than chosen here. /ʔ/ and /ʕ/ are written as nothing, which leaves a Thai zero onset correctly bare. /ħ/ is ಹ. /θ ð/ are ಥ ದ, colliding with /t̪ d/ for the dental targets, which is the documented cost. /x ɣ q/ are ಖ ಗ ಕ. /ç/ is ಖ where the target has an /x/ for it to front (German ich) and ಹ where it does not (Japanese ひ). /y yː ʉ ø œ ɵ/ are ಊ/ೂ, Kannada's long u, which is how Kannada print reads a front rounded vowel (ಮ್ಯೂನಿಕ್, ಯೂರೋ). /ɯ/ is ಉ, following the romanisation its two largest holders use -- Japanese u and Korean ㅡ. /ɤ/ is ಏ, which is what Kannada print gives Mandarin's e. /ɲ/ is ನ್ಯ and /ʎ/ ಲ್ಯ, Hindi's cluster shapes kept rather than replaced by Kannada's own ಞ and ಙ: **both letters exist and neither is written standing on its own.** ಞ appears in modern Kannada essentially only inside the conjunct ಜ್ಞ (ಜ್ಞಾನಂ, ಪ್ರಜ್ಞ) and ಙ only inside ಙ್ಕ, so a bare ಞಿ for Japanese に would be a shape a reader has not met, where ನ್ಯಿ is one they read every day. Bare /ŋ/ is ಂಗ, the anusvara plus ಗ, which is exactly how Kannada writes an English -ing: ಮಾರ್ನಿಂಗ್. Vietnamese's glottalised codas and its /ˀ/ are dropped with the tone they belong to. /ʂ ʈʂ ʈʂʰ/ keep ಷ ಚ ಛ, since Kannada ಷ is a live letter with its own retroflex value rather than Hindi's ष, which Hindi speakers read as [ʃ]. Korean's /ɰ/ and Mandarin's /ɥ/ are ವ and ಯ.
note:
**Kannada is an abugida, so the design decision in this table is where the virama goes**, and it is Telugu's decision because it is the same problem: a consonant letter with nothing after it already says [a], so a cluster that forgets its virama does not merely look wrong -- it prints a vowel the target does not have. Every consonant therefore has three spellings and `spellSlot`'s position decides between them: bare when it is the first thing in the syllable (`after_out: ""`), so a vowel sign can bind to it; virama-then-letter anywhere else in an onset, joining it to the consonant before; and letter-then-virama in a coda, killing its own inherent vowel. The two directions are not interchangeable and a slot cannot look ahead within itself, which is why the choice is made on what has already been emitted.

**What Kannada adds to that mechanism, and what a reader should know before trusting the column.** Kannada stacks in *both* directions and it has a third device Telugu does not. The virama-then-letter form is not a sequence of two glyphs: the shaper turns it into a **subscript** consonant hung below the line, so `್ಕ` after a letter draws as a small ಕ beneath it, and there is no codepoint for any of the 34 subscript forms -- they are reached only through GSUB. On top of that, a **coda `ರ್` followed by a consonant becomes the arkavattu**, a superscript hook drawn over the *following* letter (ಕರ್ನಾಟಕ), which is a rendering of the same codepoints and needs nothing from this table. Both are invisible here and load-bearing for the font build -- see `KNDA_RANGES` in scripts/subset_fonts.py -- and together they are why the `Knda` leading factor is what it is. One consequence a reader will see: at a syllable break a coda `ರ್` has no following consonant to ride over, so it draws with a visible virama (`ವರ್-ಕ್` for *work*) rather than as an arkavattu. That is legible Kannada and it is what Telugu's own coda `ర్` does.

**A Kannada consonant carries one vowel sign**, so a vowel in hiatus takes its independent letter -- the 64 hiatus rules inherited from Telugu, which found the defect on Vietnamese `biệt` and Ukrainian `hryvnia`. And **the bare-aspiration fallback is absent**: Hindi maps `ʰ` and `ʱ` to nothing, so an aspirate it has no rule for is silently spelt as its plain stop while `--gaps` reports nothing; Telugu removed the fallback and every aspirate the corpus produces has a rule of its own here, with Kannada's own ಖ ಘ ಛ ಝ ಠ ಢ ಥ ಧ ಫ ಭ. `ʲ`, `ˀ`, `ː` and `̃` keep their map-to-nothing rules, because those are *decisions*.
